title: Mailroom parcel pile
hero: ivory card parcel on a graphite mailroom counter
start: A single ivory card parcel about the size of a paperback sits on a long matte graphite mailroom counter at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. The box has crisp folded corners, a faint fibre texture and a blank label squared on its lid, and it is tied with a thin acid-lime strap that marks it as the first delivery still waiting to be sorted. Behind it, a wall of graphite pigeonholes with chamfered edges stands empty in tidy rows. To the left, a small frosted acrylic intake chute slopes down to the counter, its milky lip catching soft light. To the right, a brushed graphite trolley waits with its wheels aligned. A little paper dust sits in the counter seams. Everything is quiet, squared and ready.
end: The same mailroom counter is now buried. Ivory card parcels pour out of the frosted acrylic chute on the left in a steady frozen stream, tumbling end over end in mid-air. They have stacked into a leaning pile that fills the counter and has spilled onto the trolley, whose wheels are skewed sideways under the load. The graphite pigeonholes behind are jammed with boxes wedged in at angles, and the side panels of the pigeonhole wall bow outward, fasteners popping loose. The first parcel with its acid-lime strap is visible at the bottom of the pile, crushed flat. Corners are dented, blank labels peel, and a haze of card dust and loose packing scraps hangs over the pile, every trail leading back to the chute.
apocalypse: A long miniature valley seen from a high ridge, its floor filled by a vast landslide of weathered ivory parcels, some the size of houses, crushed into terraced sediment layers along the valley walls. At the head of the valley, the giant frosted acrylic intake chute juts from a cliff, cracked and clouded, still aimed downhill. Snapped graphite pigeonhole frames poke from the slope like the ribs of a collapsed building. The boxes are bleached, softened at the corners and seamed with fine dust. In the foreground, a slim graphite gantry on splayed legs straddles the rubble, feeding recovered parcels onto an acid-lime sorting chute that splits into three neat lanes, each lane ending in a short tidy row of boxes on the clean valley floor below. Mist fills the distance.

title: Badge reader standoff
hero: graphite badge reader beside a frosted glass door
start: A pale neutral tabletop holds a miniature doorway: a frosted glass door panel about the height of a tall book, set in a brushed graphite frame with chamfered edges and a slim steel pull handle. Mounted on the frame to the right is a small matte graphite badge reader, square and flat, with a single acid-lime indicator lens that glows faintly, still deciding. In front of the reader, one ivory card badge hangs on a thin paper lanyard from a graphite hook, its front a blank label. The door is closed, and soft light passes through the sandblasted glass. A second badge rests flat on the floor in front of the threshold. Fine dust lines the bottom of the frame. Everything is neat, with one badge waiting.
end: The same frosted glass door stays shut in its graphite frame. The badge reader's acid-lime lens has dimmed to a dull flat disc, refusing every card. In front of it, a long queue of ivory card badges on paper lanyards stretches back across the tabletop, hanging from a row of graphite hooks that has been extended in a hurry and now sags in the middle. Badges at the front are pressed against the reader, bent and creased at the corners. Behind them, more badges have slid off the hooks and piled against the threshold in a heap that pushes on the glass, which shows a fine fresh crack. One lanyard is caught mid-swing, and card dust drifts down from the pile toward the reader.
apocalypse: A wide fog-filled valley at dawn, seen low across a floor of weathered ivory badge cards compacted into drifts like fallen leaves. Rising from the fog is the building-sized ruin of the door frame, its brushed graphite uprights bent and one corner collapsed, the frosted glass panel shattered into milky shards half buried in the drifts. Twisted paper lanyards trail across the ground, bleached and frayed. The old reader lies cracked at the base of the frame. In the midground, a slim graphite tracked crawler with a folding arm is bolting a new reader onto the standing upright, its acid-lime lens lit steady, and beside it a narrow graphite gate on rails has just swung open, clearing a lane through the card drifts toward the hazy hills.

title: Projector aspect mismatch
hero: graphite projector and ivory paper screen
start: A compact matte graphite projector about the size of a toaster sits on the left of a pale neutral tabletop, its lens barrel machined with fine rings and its vents crisp. It casts a soft beam to the right onto a small freestanding screen of stretched ivory paper on a slim graphite stand. The projected image is a simple arrangement of soft pale rectangles, but its right edge runs a finger width past the screen and lands on the backdrop behind. Around the screen sits a thin acid-lime frame outline, marking the area the image is meant to fill. A folded ivory card lies beside the projector, and faint dust floats in the beam. Everything else is calm and aligned.
end: The same graphite projector has tilted back on one foot, its lens now pointing high. The beam has swollen far beyond the ivory paper screen: pale rectangles slide across the backdrop, bend over its top edge and stretch across the tabletop in warped trapezoids. The acid-lime frame around the screen still marks the correct size, now holding only a small corner of the image. The paper screen itself has bowed forward and torn from one top clip, its free corner frozen mid-flap, and its graphite stand is sliding sideways. Folded cards stacked nearby have been knocked over by the tipping projector and fan across the table. Dust churns in the brightened beam, every distortion traceable back to the lens.
apocalypse: A vast salt flat, bright and cracked into pale polygons, stretches to a sharp horizon under a flat sky. On the left, the building-sized graphite projector lies on its side, lens barrel half buried in crusted salt, vents choked with drifted grit. Across the flat stretches the torn ivory paper screen like a collapsed canopy, draped between two leaning graphite poles, its surface weathered, frayed and scored by wind, with scraps pinned in the salt crust far into the distance. In the midground, a slim graphite rail cart carrying a tall acid-lime tensioning frame is re-stretching one clean panel of the screen, its clamps pulling the paper taut and square, while a small frosted acrylic lens on a graphite tripod aims a narrow beam that fits the panel exactly.

title: Shredder jam
hero: graphite desktop shredder
start: A desktop paper shredder about the size of a shoebox sits centre frame on a pale neutral tabletop. Its head is matte graphite with chamfered corners and a row of hex fasteners, and it rests on a frosted acrylic bin whose milky walls show a small soft pile of ivory strips inside. A single ivory sheet is half fed into the slot, slightly skewed. The feed slot is lined with a thin acid-lime guide lip, the one part meant to keep sheets straight. To the left, a neat short stack of sheets waits on a graphite tray, and to the right a spare bin lid leans against the machine. Fine paper fibres cling to the slot edges. The scene is still and orderly, apart from the skewed page.
end: The same graphite shredder is now jammed and bulging. The skewed sheet has crumpled into the slot and bent the acid-lime guide lip upward. Behind it, the waiting stack has been fed in too fast and is caught half inside, pleated like a fan. Ivory paper strips burst out of every seam, from the gap between head and bin, from the vent slots and from under the base, frozen mid-spray in curling fountains. The frosted acrylic bin is overfull, its walls pushed apart, and strips spill across the tabletop in a wide fan to the right, slipping off the table edge. The graphite tray on the left has tipped and slid toward the machine. Fibre dust hangs in the air, every trajectory leading back to the jammed slot.
apocalypse: A broad windswept plain under a low grey sky is covered in rolling drifts of weathered ivory paper strips that ripple like tundra grass toward a far horizon. Near the centre rises the building-sized graphite shredder ruin, split open along its seams, its cutting head exposed and scaled with dull grit, bleached strips still caught in the fallen blades. Its frosted acrylic bin lies cracked nearby, clouded and filled with drift. The strips have matted into layers, wind-combed in one direction. In the foreground, a slim graphite tracked compactor with an acid-lime press plate is working across one drift, leaving behind a tidy row of dense, square ivory bales bound with thin graphite bands and a clean strip of bare ground in its wake.

title: Sticky-note wall collapse
hero: frosted acrylic wall panel of square paper notes
start: A freestanding frosted acrylic wall panel about the height of a laptop screen stands upright at the back of a pale neutral tabletop, held by two brushed graphite feet with chamfered fasteners. On it, a dozen small square ivory paper notes sit in three neat rows, each with a gentle curl at its lower edge and a blank front. One note in the top row is acid-lime, the priority everyone agreed on. A slim graphite rail along the bottom holds a tidy pad of fresh notes and a graphite marker lying flat. In front, the tabletop is bare. Fine fibres show along the note edges, and a few corners are very slightly lifting away from the acrylic.
end: The same frosted acrylic panel is now shingled edge to edge with ivory notes layered on notes, many deep, the mass thick and heavy. Under that weight the whole skin has peeled away from the top of the panel and is curling forward in one great sheet, caught mid-fall with its lower edge still stuck. Hundreds of loose notes flutter free from the curl, spinning in the air and settling in a spreading drift across the tabletop. The acid-lime priority note has slid under the pile and shows only one corner. The graphite rail has bent downward, the fresh pad has fanned open, and one graphite foot has lifted off the table as the panel tips forward. Paper dust hangs in the light.
apocalypse: A steep mountain cirque seen from below, where a long scree slope of weathered ivory notes pours down from a broken ridge line, the squares compacted into flaky layers and scattered boulders of fused paper. Rising from the slope is the snapped, building-sized frosted acrylic wall panel, clouded and cracked, leaning against the rock with one graphite foot jutting into the air. Wind has curled the loose notes into small drifts, their edges bleached and frayed. At the base of the slope, a slim graphite climbing rail runs straight up the fallen panel, and a small carriage with acid-lime suction pads is lifting notes one at a time from the scree and pressing them back onto the panel in three clean rows, the restored patch bright against the ruin.

title: Report nobody reads
hero: bound ivory report on a graphite delivery tray
start: A bound ivory report about the size of a paperback lies squarely on a brushed graphite delivery tray at the foot of a closed frosted glass door on a pale neutral tabletop. The report has a crisp card cover, a blank label and a tight graphite comb spine, with a single acid-lime ribbon bookmark tucked in at the first page, where the summary begins. The door, set in a slim graphite frame, lets soft light through its sandblasted panel. To the left, a small graphite wall rack stands empty. A thin skin of dust already sits on the tray lip, and the cover edge is slightly curled. Everything else is tidy and precisely placed, waiting to be picked up.
end: The same frosted glass door is still closed. In front of it the graphite delivery tray is buried under a leaning column of identical ivory reports, and more columns rise on either side, some taller than the door handle. New reports are frozen mid-drop from above, arriving on schedule and landing on the stacks. The lowest reports have yellowed, their covers curled and greyed with dust, while the newest stay crisp. The acid-lime ribbon of the first report hangs out from the bottom of the central stack, untouched and pinned flat. One column has started to topple, its upper third sliding sideways toward the wall rack, which has been knocked askew. Puffs of dust rise where each report lands.
apocalypse: A deep narrow canyon seen from its floor, its walls built of towering stacks of weathered ivory reports layered like sandstone, spines bleached and swollen, pages fused into strata. At the canyon head stands the building-sized frosted glass door, still shut, its graphite frame warped and half sunk into the stacks, the glass clouded with grime. Drifted pages lie in soft heaps along the floor, and a thin shaft of sunlight falls from the narrow strip of sky above. In the midground, a slim graphite cable arm anchored on the canyon rim reaches down with an acid-lime gripper and lifts a single open page up into the shaft of light, where it hangs flat and clean, its blank front finally lit, the cable taut.

title: Mandatory training module
hero: graphite training console with a progress bead rail
start: A compact graphite training console about the size of a hardback book sits centre frame on a pale neutral tabletop, its top machined with a single slot. A frosted acrylic cartridge with milky edges is slotted halfway in. Along the front edge runs a slim graphite progress rail with one acid-lime bead that has slid most of the way to the right end. Behind the console, a folded ivory card manual stands open like a small tent, its pages blank. To the left, a short graphite rack holds two spare cartridges upright, and to the right a closed ivory notebook lies squared to the edge. Fine dust sits in the slot, and the bead is nearly home. Everything is still and aligned.
end: The same graphite training console now sits at the head of a long queue. Frosted acrylic policy cartridges line up behind it in a winding row across the tabletop, each pushed against the next, and new ones are frozen mid-slide down a graphite chute from the left rack, which has tipped over. The current cartridge has been ejected and flies up out of the slot, spinning. On the progress rail, the acid-lime bead has been flung back to the far left end, and a bright scuff shows its fast return. The tented ivory manual has collapsed flat under a falling cartridge, and more manuals fan open around it. Milky acrylic chips and dust scatter where cartridges collide, all traceable to the ejecting slot.
apocalypse: A wide hilly terrain of terraced ivory card slopes seen from a high angle, laid out like a ruined obstacle course: collapsed graphite hurdles, a broken frosted acrylic wall, a sagging ramp and a pit filled with weathered cartridges, clouded and cracked. The building-sized training console lies tilted in a hollow, its slot choked with sediment and its progress rail snapped and dangling. Folded manuals the size of barns have slumped into the hillsides. A dusty haze hangs over the distant ridges. Across the whole course, a slim graphite rail-laying machine is putting down a single straight acid-lime track, running from the foreground over every obstacle toward the horizon, with a small graphite carriage already rolling along the finished section.

title: Survey fatigue
hero: ivory survey card in a graphite inbox tray
start: A shallow brushed graphite inbox tray palm-sized sits front left on a pale neutral tabletop, holding a single ivory survey card printed with a grid of small blank tick boxes and one acid-lime corner tab that marks it as answered. To the right stands a slim frosted acrylic drop box with a milky slot on top, empty and glowing softly. A graphite paperclip rests on the tray rim. Behind, a second empty tray waits on a short graphite riser. The card has crisp edges and a faint fibre grain, and a thin line of dust sits along the tray's machined lip. One more survey card is just visible sliding in from the back edge of the frame.
end: The same graphite inbox tray is overwhelmed. Ivory survey cards pour in from the back edge in a frozen cascade, fanning through the air and heaping over both trays until the riser has buckled and tipped forward. The frosted acrylic drop box is stuffed so full that cards jut from its slot and bulge its thin walls. Nearly every card is blank, its tick boxes untouched. The single answered card with the acid-lime tab is sinking into the pile, only its corner still showing. Cards slide off the table edge in a sheet, and a haze of dust rises where they land. The paperclip has been flicked into the air, and every card trail points back to the source edge.
apocalypse: A broad glacier of compacted ivory survey cards winds down a mountain valley toward a hazy lowland, its surface split by crevasses that expose layered strata of blank cards. Locked into the pale mass are the building-sized ruins of the frosted acrylic drop box, cracked and clouded, and the tilted graphite trays, one lip snapped off. Wind has sculpted the card surface into sharp ridges with bleached, frayed edges. In the foreground, a slim graphite sled rig on long skids works slowly across the glacier with a thin probing arm, plucking out the rare answered cards, recognisable by their marked tick boxes, and filing them upright into an acid-lime collecting rack on its back, which is already half full.

title: Review form maze
hero: short ivory review form on a graphite clipboard
start: A single sheet of ivory card sits centre frame on a pale neutral tabletop, printed with a short grid of six blank boxes in fine graphite lines. It rests on a brushed graphite clipboard with a chamfered clip and two small hex fasteners. Beside it on the right lies a slim graphite pen with its cap off, and an acid-lime handled check stamp with a clean front, the one tool meant to close the review. Behind, a shallow frosted acrylic tray holds nothing. One corner of the form is lifted where a second page has started to peek out from beneath. Fine fibre texture and a trace of eraser dust sit on the card. The arrangement is minimal and calm.
end: The same graphite clipboard is now smothered in pages. The short form has sprouted sheet after sheet of grids, each page divided into smaller and smaller blank boxes, and the stack has spread off the clipboard into a sprawling layered mat across the tabletop. New pages are frozen mid-unfold, flipping upward from the stack. The frosted tray is overfilled and tilted. The graphite pen has rolled to the table edge and hangs half over it. The acid-lime check stamp lies trapped under a fold of grids, never used, only its handle showing. Creases, torn perforations and a light haze of card dust run outward in rings from the clipboard, where the first form sits buried.
apocalypse: A high windswept plateau seen at a low angle, covered in a sprawling ruined maze whose walls are weathered ivory card sheets standing on edge, printed with faded grids of blank boxes, some walls slumped into heaps. At its centre lies the building-sized graphite clipboard, cracked across, its clip snapped upright like a broken gate. Tufts of loose fibre grow along the corridor floors, and dust gathers in the dead ends. Distant ridges fade into haze. In the foreground, a line of slim graphite survey stakes topped with acid-lime caps has been driven through the maze along one clear route, and a small graphite tracked marker rig is painting a thin lime path line between them toward the clipboard.

title: Reorg shuffle
hero: frosted acrylic org chart sculpture
start: A small org chart sculpture about the size of a dinner plate stands centre frame on a pale neutral tabletop. Frosted acrylic cubes, each the size of a sugar cube and glowing softly at their milky edges, are arranged in three tidy tiers and joined by slim brushed graphite rods seated in machined sockets. The top cube sits in an acid-lime socket collar that holds the whole structure level. Blank ivory card tags hang from each cube on thin threads. To the left, a spare graphite rod and two spare cubes lie in a shallow tray, and one cube in the lower tier sits slightly out of line. Fine dust rests on the base plate. The whole chart is neat and symmetrical.
end: The same org chart is mid-shuffle. Frosted acrylic cubes are frozen in the air, being swapped between tiers, while others slide across the base plate in new directions. Several graphite rods have snapped at their sockets and hang loose, swinging, and a couple have flown out to land across the tabletop. The acid-lime collar at the top has been knocked off its cube and rolls on its edge toward the tray. Blank ivory tags have tangled together in a knot, and some have torn free and drift down. The spare tray on the left has been emptied and tipped. Acrylic chips and a fine haze of dust spread outward from the base plate, which has slipped toward the table edge.
apocalypse: A wide overgrown plain of long pale grass stretches to low hills, seen from a low angle in soft morning haze. Scattered across it are house-sized frosted acrylic cubes, toppled, cracked and clouded, some half sunk into the soil with grass growing from their fractures. Snapped graphite rods lie like fallen masts between them, and faded ivory tags hang in tatters from their ends. The tilted base plate forms a cracked platform on the left. In the midground, a slim graphite tower crane with an acid-lime hook block is lowering one cube onto a small new structure of just three cubes joined by short straight rods, a simple chart rising in a cleared patch of trimmed grass.

title: Budget reallocation
hero: graphite distributor wheel over token bins
start: Three shallow ivory card bins with crisp folded corners sit in a row on a pale neutral tabletop, each resting on a small brushed graphite scale pan with a plain dial with tick marks at its base. The bins hold neat stacks of frosted acrylic tokens, coin-sized with milky edges. Above them, a slim graphite distributor wheel about the height of a mug, ringed with small scoop cups, sits ready to move tokens between bins. A single acid-lime token rests in the middle bin, the reserve nobody should touch. All three dials read level. One token on the left stack has been nudged slightly off-centre. Fine dust lines the scale pans. The layout is balanced and precise.
end: The same distributor wheel is spinning fast, frozen mid-rotation, its scoop cups flinging frosted acrylic tokens from bin to bin in overlapping arcs through the air. The left ivory bin is overflowing, tokens spilling over its folded edge and bouncing across the tabletop; its scale pan has sunk to the table and its dial needle is pinned past the last tick. The right bin is nearly empty, its pan jerked upward. The middle bin has torn at one corner. The acid-lime reserve token has been scooped out and tumbles in mid-air above the wheel. Loose tokens roll toward the table edge, and card fibres and acrylic dust drift from the tear, every arc tracing back to the wheel.
apocalypse: A dry, cracked riverbed winds through a wide sediment valley, its banks layered in pale bands, toward a hazy horizon. Standing in the dry channel is the building-sized graphite distributor wheel, seized solid, its scoop cups cracked and choked with silt. Enormous frosted acrylic tokens lie strewn along the bed like river stones, clouded and chipped. The three giant ivory bins have collapsed on the bank, one sagging open, one flattened, one half buried, their scale dials dusted over. In the midground, a slim graphite tripod rig carries a long acid-lime balancing beam, and small graphite arms at each end are placing tokens into two rebuilt bins, the beam hanging perfectly level between them.

title: Vendor onboarding forms
hero: vendor form packet on a graphite clipboard
start: A brushed graphite clipboard about the size of a tablet lies at a slight angle on a pale neutral tabletop, holding a thin packet of four ivory paper forms with crisp edges and faint lines of blank fields. Its chamfered clip is closed on the packet, and a single acid-lime tab marks the signature page as the only step left. To the right, a frosted acrylic document tray waits empty. Behind the clipboard, a small ivory card box of blank tabbed dividers stands upright. A slim graphite pen lies parallel to the clipboard. Along the top edge of the packet, a second loose form is just starting to slip in beneath the clip. Fibre grain and pencil dust show on the paper. Everything is calm.
end: The same graphite clipboard can no longer hold the packet. The forms have multiplied into a tall, leaning tower of ivory sheets many times the clipboard's height, pinned only at the base by the straining clip, which is bent open. The tower bows to the right, and its upper third is frozen mid-collapse, sheets peeling off in slow fans and gliding toward the frosted tray, which is already overfilled and cracked at one corner. The acid-lime signature tab is visible deep in the lower stack, squeezed flat. The divider box has been knocked over, spilling blank tabs. The graphite pen is skidding away. Dust and paper fibres swirl in the air, and the lean points straight back to the clip.
apocalypse: A rolling desert of ivory paper dunes, each dune built from layered weathered forms with wind-frayed edges, stretches toward a shimmering horizon under a hard low sun. Half buried on a dune crest is the building-sized graphite clipboard, its clip snapped and jutting upward like a broken arch, pale fibre drifting over it. The frosted acrylic tray lies cracked in a hollow, filled with paper sediment. Ripples of loose sheets cross the slopes. In the midground, a slim graphite crawler with a long boom carries an acid-lime binding clamp, which is gathering one small, neat packet of forms from the dune slope and pressing it square and tight between its jaws, leaving a flattened clean trail behind.

title: Tool migration
hero: graphite truss bridge between two system blocks
start: Two system blocks sit on a pale neutral tabletop about a short span apart. On the left is a heavy matte graphite block the size of a brick, its sides machined with shallow grooves and old scuffs. On the right is a new frosted acrylic block of the same size, glowing softly at its milky edges. Between them spans a slim graphite truss bridge carrying a small conveyor belt, and a line of tiny ivory card data blocks moves across it in single file. The bridge rests on an acid-lime centre pin that carries all the load. The first few data blocks have arrived neatly on the frosted side. Fine dust sits on the old block. Everything is orderly and aligned.
end: The same truss bridge now sags in the middle, its acid-lime centre pin sheared and hanging from one side. The belt has slumped into a V, and ivory data blocks tumble off both edges, frozen in mid-air at every height between the two systems. A heap of blocks has formed on the tabletop in the gap, some cracked open, some stacked crookedly. The graphite block on the left keeps pushing more blocks onto the broken belt. On the right, the frosted acrylic block has slid back slightly, and the few blocks that arrived have toppled over. Dust rises from the pile, and a scatter of blocks bounces toward the camera, all traceable back to the sheared pin.
apocalypse: A deep rocky gorge seen from its rim, the far side a sheer cliff and a thin river of haze at the bottom. On the near rim stands the old graphite system block, now the size of a fortress, weathered and cracked; on the far rim sits the frosted acrylic block, clouded and chipped. The collapsed graphite truss bridge dangles from both edges into the gorge, bent and snapped. Far below, the gorge floor is filled with a talus of bleached ivory data blocks. In the midground, a slim graphite launching gantry on the near rim is sliding out a new acid-lime span, already reaching most of the way across, with a small graphite carriage carrying the first data block over it.

title: Stale wiki
hero: graphite shelf of ivory binders
start: A slim brushed graphite shelf about the length of a forearm is mounted on a frosted acrylic back panel on a pale neutral tabletop. On it stands a neat row of ivory card binders with crisp spines and blank label windows, upright and evenly spaced. Most are clean, but the three at the right end carry a fine grey film of dust along their tops. The newest binder, in the middle, has a single acid-lime spine clip marking the current version. A graphite bookend with a chamfered edge holds the row. In front, a loose page lies front down on the tabletop, slightly curled. Fibre grain shows on each spine. The shelf is level and tidy, with only the dust out of place.
end: The same graphite shelf sags hard at the centre, its bracket bending away from the frosted panel. The ivory binders have yellowed and warped, many pushed in at odd angles with split spines. Near-duplicates crowd the row, each a slightly different shade, and loose pages spill from their rings, frozen mid-air in a slow waterfall toward the tabletop. The acid-lime spine clip of the current binder has popped free and is tumbling downward. The graphite bookend has slid off the end and lies on its side. On the tabletop, pages from different binders have piled into overlapping, contradictory layers. Dust puffs from the falling binders, and every loose page traces back to the dip in the shelf.
apocalypse: A shallow flooded basin under an overcast sky, its calm grey water reflecting the ruins of a vast collapsed library. Giant ivory binders, swollen and yellowed, stand half submerged like leaning towers, their spines split and bleached, pages drifting in soft rafts on the surface. The building-sized graphite shelf lies snapped across the basin like a fallen bridge, and the frosted acrylic back panel has toppled behind it, clouded and cracked. Distant binder ruins fade into mist. In the midground, a slim graphite floating rack on pontoons with an acid-lime picker arm is lifting dry current pages from a raft and filing them into a short, straight row of new binders on its deck, the row neat against the wreckage.

title: Search finds nothing
hero: graphite card-catalog cabinet with a search probe
start: A small brushed graphite card-catalog cabinet about the size of a shoebox stands centre frame on a pale neutral tabletop, with six shallow drawers, each fitted with a chamfered pull and a blank label holder. Hovering just above the cabinet on a slim graphite gantry arm is a search probe, a thin rod ending in a small acid-lime sensor tip, aimed at the top drawer. Inside the half-open top drawer, ivory index cards stand upright in tight order, their tabs unmarked. To the left, a shallow frosted acrylic tray waits for results, empty. The probe is angled very slightly toward the wrong drawer. Fine dust rests on the cabinet top. The scene is precise and still.
end: The same graphite cabinet has every drawer yanked open, several pulled right out and hanging from their runners. The gantry probe has swung wildly off target, its acid-lime sensor tip jammed into the bottom drawer at a steep angle. Ivory index cards spray out of the drawers in frozen arcs, fanning across the tabletop in overlapping drifts. One drawer has fallen completely, spilling a long slide of cards toward the camera. The frosted acrylic results tray is still empty but has been knocked sideways. Cards are creased, bent at the tabs and scattered front up and front down. A thin haze of card dust hangs over the cabinet, every arc tracing back to the misaimed probe.
apocalypse: A wide tidal mudflat at low tide, sheened with shallow water and cut by winding channels, reaches toward a pale horizon. Spread across it is a vast spilled delta of weathered ivory index cards, fanned out in lobes like river sediment, their edges softened and bleached. The building-sized graphite cabinet lies tipped on its back at the head of the delta, drawers hanging open like broken steps, runners bent. The old probe gantry leans snapped over it. In the midground, a long slim graphite index rail on stilts runs straight across the flats, and a small shuttle with an acid-lime sorting head moves along it, picking cards from the mud and slotting them into a clean, ordered row along the rail.

title: Broken link
hero: chain of ivory page tiles joined by graphite links
start: A chain of five ivory card page tiles, each about the size of a playing card with crisp edges and blank fronts, runs left to right across a pale neutral tabletop on small graphite stands. The tiles are joined by short brushed graphite links with machined pins, except the link between the third and fourth tile, which is acid-lime and already hairline cracked. A small frosted acrylic bead, the size of a pea, rolls along a narrow groove through the chain from left to right, and a second bead waits at the start. The tiles are evenly spaced and level. A faint line of dust marks the groove. Everything is calm, with the one weak link easy to find.
end: The same chain of ivory page tiles has split at the acid-lime link, which has snapped in two, its halves swinging downward on their pins. The third and fourth tiles have tilted away from each other, opening a gap. Frosted acrylic beads keep arriving along the groove from the left and pour straight off the broken end, frozen in a falling column into the gap and scattering across the tabletop below. A pile of beads has built up beneath the break and has started pushing the fourth tile's stand sideways. The last two tiles, still linked, sit stranded and empty. Dust and tiny acrylic chips spray outward, and the bead trail traces cleanly back to the first tile.
apocalypse: A vast chasm splits a high rocky plateau, its walls layered in pale sediment and dropping into deep blue haze. Across it once ran a monorail of giant ivory page tiles on graphite pylons; now the line ends in a jagged break on both sides, the tile sections weathered, bleached and cracked, and the old snapped link hanging in pieces. Far below, a drift of clouded frosted acrylic beads the size of boulders fills the chasm floor. The remaining tiles stretch away along the plateau toward the horizon. At the break, a slim graphite cantilever crane anchored on the near edge is lowering a single acid-lime rail section into the gap on taut cables, its ends only a short drop from the pylons.

title: Cache not cleared
hero: frosted glass display case holding an old page model
start: A small display case about the height of a mug stands centre frame on a pale neutral tabletop, a box of sandblasted frosted glass framed in thin brushed graphite with chamfered corners. Inside, an older ivory card page model, slightly yellowed with softened folds, stands on a graphite plinth facing out. Just to the right, outside the case, waits a new crisp ivory page model on its own plinth, its edges sharp, marked with a single acid-lime corner tab to show it is the current version. A small hinged graphite door on the back of the case is closed. Fine dust sits on the top pane. The two models look alike but not quite the same. Everything is aligned and still.
end: The same frosted display case is now crammed. Behind the old yellowed page model, new versions have been pushed in through the rear door one after another, leaning in a tight overlapping stack that presses against the back glass until it bows and cracks. The newest model with its acid-lime corner tab is wedged at the very back, barely visible. The old model remains upright at the front, unmoved, dust thick on its top edge. More new models are frozen mid-slide toward the rear door from the right, some crumpling as they hit the jam. The rear door hangs open on one hinge. Glass grit and card dust fall onto the tabletop, all the pressure pushing up against the old model.
apocalypse: A wide ash-pale dust basin under a flat sky, where fine drifted powder lies over everything in soft rounded dunes toward distant hills. In the centre stands the building-sized ruin of the display case, its graphite frame bent and its sandblasted glass walls filmed with thick dust, one pane collapsed. Inside, the giant old ivory page model still stands at the front, bleached and brittle, while dozens of newer versions have slumped into a heap behind it. In the foreground, a slim graphite gantry with a long acid-lime wiper blade sweeps across the front pane, clearing a clean bright band through the dust, and a small graphite arm reaches through the broken rear to lift the newest page model forward.

title: Works on my machine
hero: graphite desk rig with a frosted acrylic gear train
start: A small desk rig about the size of a shoebox stands on the left of a pale neutral tabletop: a brushed graphite platform carrying a tidy mechanism of three frosted acrylic gears and a short graphite lever, meshed perfectly. The centre gear is acid-lime, the drive gear everything depends on. A thin graphite shim sits under one corner of the platform, keeping it level. On the right, a second, near-identical graphite platform waits empty, with slightly different mounting holes and no shim. A folded ivory card with a blank front rests between them. Fine dust sits in the gear teeth, and a faint polish on the axles shows long smooth running. The working rig is calm and precise.
end: The mechanism has been moved onto the second platform on the right, and it is coming apart. Without the shim, the platform tilts, and the frosted acrylic gears have slipped out of mesh; one is frozen mid-roll off the edge, another is jammed at an angle with a chipped tooth. The acid-lime drive gear has jumped its axle and spins alone in mid-air above the platform. The graphite lever has snapped out and bounces across the tabletop. Screws and small graphite pins scatter from the misaligned mounting holes. On the left, the original platform sits empty and level, its shim still in place. Acrylic chips and dust spray outward from the tilted platform, traceable to the missing shim.
apocalypse: A badlands landscape of layered sediment mesas under a hazy sky, cut by a deep dry ravine. On the left mesa stands the towering original graphite platform, level and weathered; on the right mesa, its twin leans at a visible slant, one corner sunk into cracked ground. Giant frosted acrylic gears, clouded and chipped, lie scattered down the ravine slopes, one wedged across the gap. The old lever lies snapped on the ravine floor, and wind has scoured grooves into the mesa sides. In the midground, a slim graphite jacking rig slides acid-lime shims under the low corner of the right platform, raising it, while a taut graphite level line stretched between the two tops shows them nearly matched.

title: Placeholder shipped
hero: placeholder layout block on a graphite conveyor
start: A short brushed graphite conveyor about the length of a ruler runs left to right across a pale neutral tabletop, its belt matte and finely ribbed. On it sits a single ivory card layout block the size of a paperback, its front covered in flat graphite-grey placeholder bars and a crossed-out image rectangle, nothing real yet. At the right end of the belt, a slim graphite shipping gate stands open. Behind the conveyor, a frosted acrylic tray holds the finished content card, held by a single acid-lime clip, waiting to replace the placeholder. The belt is still. Fine card dust sits along the rollers, and a faint scuff marks where the block was set down. Everything is neat and square.
end: The same graphite conveyor is running fast. Layout blocks covered in graphite-grey placeholder bars stream off the right end through the shipping gate, frozen in mid-air as they launch off the belt and tumble into a growing heap on the tabletop beyond, some sliding off the table edge. More placeholder blocks keep appearing on the left and bunch up, overlapping. The frosted acrylic tray behind has been knocked over by the vibrating frame, and the finished content card with its acid-lime clip lies front down under the belt, missed entirely. The belt has frayed at one edge. Card dust and grey flecks scatter in the air, every block trajectory leading back to the open gate.
apocalypse: A vast terraced quarry cut into pale sediment cliffs, its steps stretching into a hazy distance. Scattered across every terrace are enormous weathered ivory blocks bearing faded graphite-grey placeholder bars, some upright like monoliths, some toppled and cracked, some half buried in rubble. The building-sized conveyor lies broken along the top terrace, its belt torn and hanging over the edge like a ribbon, and the shipping gate is snapped. In the midground, a slim graphite gantry on rails straddles a row of blocks and lowers an acid-lime stamping head onto one, pressing a finished content front into it, while three already stamped blocks stand clean and upright behind it in a short tidy line.

title: Heavy page
hero: ivory page tile loaded with frosted glass image slabs
start: A single ivory card page tile about the size of a paperback spans two slim brushed graphite supports on a pale neutral tabletop, like a small bridge. Resting on it are three thick sandblasted frosted glass image slabs, each far heavier than the page, stacked slightly off-centre. The page already dips a fraction in the middle. At the right end, a small graphite loading track leads away, and a single acid-lime speed bead sits at its start, waiting to travel. To the left, a thin, light ivory card image lies unused on the table. Fine grit sits on the glass edges, and the card shows faint fibre grain. The setup is quiet and clean.
end: The same page tile is bowing deeply between its graphite supports, its card fibres stretched and creasing along a long central fold. The frosted glass slabs have slid toward the sag and collided, one cracked across its corner, another tipping over the edge and frozen mid-fall. More glass slabs have been added on top, stacked high. One graphite support has buckled inward. On the loading track, the acid-lime speed bead has barely crept a thumb's width and is stuck. The light ivory card image still lies unused to the left. Glass grit sprays across the tabletop from the cracked slab, and card fibres hang from a tear starting at the centre, all the load tracing back to the stack.
apocalypse: A wide impact crater in a pale ivory landscape, its rim raised and layered, seen from a high angle with low hills beyond. At the centre lies the crushed building-sized page tile, folded into the ground in a deep V, its fibres torn and bleached, pinned under a heap of giant frosted glass slabs, cracked and clouded. Buckled graphite supports stick out of the crater walls, and glass shards glint in the dust. On the rim, a slim graphite gantry press with an acid-lime compressor head lifts one slab, squeezes it into a thin, light panel, and sets it onto a clean new page tile resting flat on two short graphite supports, which stays perfectly level under the load.

title: Form to nowhere
hero: web page model with a form slot and frosted pipe
start: A miniature web page model stands upright on a pale neutral tabletop: an ivory card panel about the size of a tablet, held in a brushed graphite frame, with a neat input slot cut into its lower half and a blank button panel below it. From the back of the slot, a slim frosted acrylic pipe runs out behind the page, curves to the right and ends in an acid-lime coupling that connects to nothing. A single folded ivory submission card is frozen halfway into the slot. On the right, an empty graphite inbox tray sits a short distance from the pipe end. Fine dust lines the slot edge. Everything is tidy, with the gap small but visible.
end: The same page model is receiving submissions quickly. Folded ivory cards are pushed through its slot one after another, and inside the milky frosted acrylic pipe a dense column of cards can be seen sliding along. At the acid-lime coupling they drop out of the open end, frozen mid-fall, and pile up in a spreading heap on the tabletop, well short of the empty graphite inbox tray on the right, which stays clean. The heap has grown so wide that it presses against the page frame and has tilted it backward. Some cards burst open as they land. Card dust drifts from the pipe mouth, and every card in the heap traces back through the pipe to the slot.
apocalypse: A wide marshy estuary under a low sky, where reed beds of pale ivory paper fronds line shallow grey pools that reach toward a sea haze. At the edge of the marsh, the building-sized frosted acrylic pipe juts from the mud, cracked and clouded, its end broken off. Beneath its mouth, a vast pool of weathered submission cards has settled into soft sodden layers, bleached and swollen, with reeds growing through them. The fallen page model lies front up in the distance, its frame warped. In the midground, a slim graphite pipe-laying rig on tracks is fitting a new acid-lime pipe section onto the broken end, bending it toward a clean graphite inbox tray on a raised platform.

title: Staging vs production
hero: twin graphite platforms
start: Two identical brushed graphite platforms, each about the size of a small book, sit side by side on a pale neutral tabletop a short span apart. Each carries the same arrangement: a frosted acrylic block, a folded ivory card sign with a blank front and a small graphite lever. The only difference is a thin acid-lime band wrapped around the base of the right platform, marking it as production. Between them, a slim graphite push arm on a pivot rests over the left platform, loaded with a new ivory card component. Fine machining marks and a light layer of dust are visible on both. The two setups mirror each other exactly, and everything is calm.
end: The graphite push arm has swung the wrong way, over to the right platform with the acid-lime band, and is ramming its new ivory card component straight into the production setup. The frosted acrylic block there has been knocked off and is frozen mid-tumble toward the table edge, and the folded sign is crushed flat under the component. The graphite lever has sprung loose and flies upward. More components queued on the arm are sliding forward to follow. Meanwhile the left platform stays untouched and pristine. A crack runs through the right platform's base, and acrylic chips and card dust burst outward from the impact, every fragment pointing back to the pivot.
apocalypse: Two matching ruins stand on opposite banks of a wide tidal channel, seen from a coastal headland as sea mist rolls in. Each is a building-sized graphite platform, weathered and streaked, carrying a cracked frosted acrylic block and a slumped ivory card sign. The right ruin is more broken, its block toppled into the channel and its base split through, the old band worn down to bleached bare metal. Banks of paper sediment line both shores, lapped by slow water. In the midground, a slim graphite survey rig on long jointed legs is driving a tall acid-lime marker post into the base of the right ruin, picking out production clearly across the water for anything that approaches.

title: Friday hotfix
hero: cracked graphite plate with a patch
start: A thick brushed graphite plate about the size of a coaster lies flat on a pale neutral tabletop, a machined part with chamfered edges and fine milling marks. A thin crack runs across it. Over the crack sits a small ivory card patch, taped down at its corners, and at its centre a single acid-lime rivet pins the patch in place. To the right, a tidy row of three more ivory patches and a small graphite driver tool wait on a frosted acrylic tray. To the left sits a closed ivory card lunch box, packed and ready for the weekend. Fine grit sits in the crack. Everything else is neat, and the fix looks almost good enough.
end: The same graphite plate is now split wide, the crack branching in several directions. Patch after patch has been layered over it in a hurry, ivory card squares overlapping at odd angles, some bolted, some taped, some already tearing. Small graphite bolts are frozen mid-air as the patches lift and pop them loose. The original acid-lime rivet has sheared and sits at the bottom of the widening crack. The frosted acrylic tray is empty and knocked sideways, and the driver tool has rolled away. The plate has lifted at one edge, breaking in two, and graphite fragments and card scraps spray outward, all tracing back to the first crack. The closed lunch box sits untouched on the left.
apocalypse: A vast dry lakebed of pale clay cracked into deep polygons stretches to a low horizon, with one enormous fissure running straight across it. The building-sized graphite plate lies split along that fissure, its halves tilted, its surface crusted with layers of weathered ivory card patches many deep, curled, bleached and peeling like old paint, with loose bolts scattered in the clay. Dust devils rise in the distance. In the midground, a slim graphite rig on four splayed legs is lowering a single long acid-lime brace across the fissure and bolting it to both halves, while a small graphite gauge with a plain dial with tick marks, mounted beside it, shows the gap closing.

title: QA ticket bounce
hero: ivory ticket arcing between build and QA trays
start: Two shallow brushed graphite trays front each other on a pale neutral tabletop, a forearm apart: a build tray on the left and a QA tray on the right, each with a small spring-loaded return flap at its lip. In the gap between them, a single ivory card ticket about the size of a playing card is frozen in a low, lazy arc heading right. Its front is blank except for one small circular stamp mark near the top. An acid-lime catch clip is mounted on the side of the QA tray, meant to hold the ticket once it lands. The trays are neat and aligned, and fine dust sits in the spring hinges.
end: The same ticket is bouncing between the trays at speed, frozen at the peak of a high arc, its surface now covered in overlapping blank circular stamp marks and creased at every corner. Both spring flaps have snapped up and are still vibrating, and each tray has skidded apart from repeated impacts, leaving scuff trails on the tabletop. Torn corners and card flecks from earlier bounces litter the gap below the arc. The acid-lime catch clip on the QA tray has been knocked open and hangs loose, missing every landing. A short graphite stamp handle has fallen onto its side next to the build tray. Dust puffs rise from both trays, and the arc links them.
apocalypse: A windswept heath of low pale scrub rolls toward a misty horizon. On opposite rises sit two building-sized graphite trays, weathered and dented, their spring flaps locked in the raised position and cracked at the hinges. A snapped graphite return spring lies coiled in the scrub between them. The ground in the hollow is littered with weathered ivory card flakes stamped over and over with faded circles, drifted into soft ridges. In the midground, a slim graphite mast rig on a wide base extends a long arm holding an acid-lime catch cradle, which has just closed around the giant, battered ticket in mid-air above the hollow, holding it still over the QA tray at last.

title: Sprint carryover
hero: graphite sprint tray of task cards
start: A shallow brushed graphite sprint tray about the length of a forearm sits on a pale neutral tabletop, divided into three neat lanes by thin graphite ribs. Ivory card task cards with blank fronts stand upright in the lanes, most of them already in the right lane, done. To the right, an empty second tray waits on a slim graphite rail, coupled to the first like a pair of rail wagons. One card in the left lane carries a single acid-lime tab and has not moved. Beside the trays, a closed ivory card box of fresh cards sits squared to the edge. Fine dust gathers along the ribs. Everything is calm, and the rail runs straight.
end: The graphite trays roll along their rail, now a train of several trays coupled together, and every tray is overfull. Unfinished cards have been carried from the first tray into the next and the next, piling up in leaning heaps that spill over the ribs. The acid-lime tab card is buried in the third tray, still in its left lane. The lead tray has jumped the rail and tipped at an angle, frozen mid-derailment, and cards slide off it in a fan across the tabletop. The coupling behind has snapped taut. The box of fresh cards has been emptied into the last tray. Card dust and a few airborne cards trace back along the rail to the first tray.
apocalypse: A long railway embankment crosses a snow-dusted steppe toward a pale horizon, and along it lies a derailed train of building-sized graphite trays, jackknifed, some on their sides, couplings snapped. Weathered ivory task cards have spilled from every tray into drifts along the embankment slopes, bleached and softened, settled into layers under thin snow. The first tray sits far back on the straight rails, nearly empty. In the midground, a slim graphite sorting rig on its own rail carriage lifts cards with an acid-lime sorting arm and places them upright in a single tidy lane of a clean new tray behind it, while the rest of the wrecked train waits under the snow.
